title: US Open 2026 results: How Aryna Sabalenka emotions encapsulated season of setbacks
description: Aryna Sabalenka cut a forlorn figure as she sat staring into space following a painful defeat by Elena Rybakina in the US Open final.As Rybakina celeb
body: Aryna Sabalenka cut a forlorn figure as she sat staring into space following a painful defeat by Elena Rybakina in the US Open final.As Rybakina celebrated her third Grand Slam title following a 6-4 5-7 6-2 win in New York, cameras pictured Sabalenka deep in thought as she sat in silence with her team.At a tournament which has delivered so much success for two-time champion Sabalenka, the disappointment the 28-year-old has faced in the past week leaves her with plenty to ponder.Not only has Rybakina replaced Sabalenka as the world number one after 99 weeks at the summit, she has now ended the Belarusian's 20-match winning streak at Flushing Meadows.Defeat also means Sabalenka will end the year without winning a Grand Slam title for the first time since 2022.For four-time Grand Slam singles champion Sabalenka, the disappointment was palpable.Throughout the final, faced with a composed Rybakina who put together an outstanding performance, Sabalenka could not keep her frustrations at bay.Her racquet felt the brunt of her exasperation as she slammed it to the ground after offering a break point to Rybakina in the second set.After Rybakina sent an ace past her to secure victory, Sabalenka flung her racquet away in disgust before congratulating her opponent. As Rybakina waved to the crowd, Sabalenka sat on her chair and smashed another racquet against the floor.Sabalenka also used an expletive as she told a cameraperson to go away as she sat with her team immediately after defeat."It's really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat," Sabalenka said afterwards."So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there."So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."Sabalenka is always vocal on court and has been known to berate herself and roll her eyes ironically when missing points, even in her most dominant of victories.Often she can channel her emotions into her aggressive hitting, but former British number one Annabel Croft believes it contributed to her downfall against Rybakina."It was extraordinary to witness because she had been very negative on herself with her body language in that first set and suddenly the emotions got the better of her," Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live."I felt like that really contributed to her going down in that first set. She was beating herself."Sabalenka held back tears during a post-match interview in which she praised Rybakina's performance.Croft says the Belarusian would benefit from applying the same level of poise during her matches."I think what happened was the minute she started to not respect the level of tennis her opponent was playing, she couldn't handle it at all," said Croft."You have to respect what they're putting out there and applaud it but then find ways to dig in and find another way to compete with them."It was almost like throwing the toys out of the pram today."The weight of expectation Sabalenka puts on herself has affected her in major finals in particular.She has won four of her nine Grand Slam singles finals, and only won one of her four finals as the world number one.All five of her major final losses were in three sets, and on two of those occasions Sabalenka won the opening set.After defending her US Open crown in 2025, she began this year targeting more Grand Slam success.However, she lost a tight three-set Australian Open final to Rybakina before she imploded at the French Open. Leading Russia's Diana Shnaider by a set and 4-1 in the quarter-finals, Sabalenka totally lost her way, being dragged into a decider that she lost 6-0.At Wimbledon, Sabalenka lost in the fourth round to Japanese four-time Grand Slam winner Naomi Osaka in what was her earliest Grand Slam exit for four years.Sabalenka has won three WTA titles this year, triumphing in Brisbane, Indian Wells and the Miami Open, but she has been second best to Rybakina in the hard-court majors.The US Open was meant to salvage Sabalenka's season - but she must now regroup as she adjusts to her position as world number two."I think overall I should be happy with the level I played, and there's lots of things to take from this tournament," Sabalenka said."Experience shows that I only come back stronger and all of these lessons this season definitely already made me stronger, but definitely going to motivate me for the next year to do a better job."

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: How Aryna Sabalenka emotions encapsulated season of setbacks

title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina on title win after pre-tournament injury
description: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world numb
body: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.Playing on through injury could have had dire consequences for the rest of her season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year."I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said."We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great."I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain."I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week, but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding."I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said."I still can't believe it."Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but it was Rybakina who dominated the decider.While her Belarusian opponent grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed."The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live."Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she coolly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride"."I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said."There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table."It's not going to be easy to hang on to it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1,000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times."I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina on title win after pre-tournament injury

title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
description: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation anno
body: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation announced late on Friday.Thailand-based Harborne wrote in the Telegraph, external that his "competitive spirit" inspired him to equal Ben Delo's donation - the largest ever given to a UK political party - adding he expected "nothing personally" in return.Reform said the £72m would be used to hire "the brightest and best minds to work on policy and the most comprehensive plan for government ever".The party is facing scrutiny over its finances, as the government seeks to cap donations to UK political parties from British expats.There have also been renewed calls by MPs from other political parties for donations from individuals to be capped.The £72m from the two donations is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year, which stood at just over £69m. Reform leader Nigel Farage said Harborne and Delo's "generosity" meant the party would "now be able to fight and win the next general election on a level playing field".A Reform UK spokesman added: "We will now also be able to hire up to 400 campaign managers in every target constituency. We are now on election footing."Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Saturday, the party's deputy leader Richard Tice denied accusations the donations were bad for democracy."It's the opposite actually, we're delighted and very humbled by the confidence expressed by two very successful entrepreneurs who realise Britain's in serious trouble," he said."To have that support, to know we can focus on employing the best people, whether it be on social media, policy, campaign managers, that's a good thing."Earlier, speaking to Sky News, Tice said Delo's donation had been an upfront sum "so that the Labour Party can't legislate against it" and would be spent over two or three years.Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations. The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage"."A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.However, the Labour government has introduced a £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.There were nine donations of £1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was £9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.Labour had five donations of £1m or more - totalling nearly £10m - and the Conservatives had three of £1m each.Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of £500,000.She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding:  "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over £100,000 a year.But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging £72m to one political party in less than 48 hours."This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

title: Rangers v Celtic: What makes Sunday's League Cup quarter-final crucial?
description: Celtic have won all six of their Scottish Premiership matches so far this season with 14 goals scored and just three conceded, but that does not quite
body: Celtic have won all six of their Scottish Premiership matches so far this season with 14 goals scored and just three conceded, but that does not quite tell the full story.They squeezed past Dundee at home in their first game of the season, but that was followed by rampant wins at Kilmarnock and Dundee United. Things looked even better when they put three goals past LASK without response in the first leg of their Champions League play-off, but what occurred the following week was a capitulation of the highest order. Callum McGregor's early goal in Austria had Celtic four goals to the good and heading for the league phase, but LASK mounted the comeback of all comebacks to win 5-1 on the night and 5-4 on aggregate. While the ship has steadied since then and Celtic have won all four of their following league matches, a narrow victory at St Johnstone in midweek was far from convincing, albeit manager Martin O'Neill had made significant changes to his starting line-up.Previewing Sunday's derby encounter, Celtic great Scott Brown explained the importance of a fast start in this fixture."As a Celtic player, you want to silence that crowd early doors," he said."You want to make sure that you keep the ball, you dictate, and if Celtic get an early goal it becomes a nervous Ibrox."The big [derby] is always the first game."Rangers manager Derek McInnes: "I think we've got to bring the crowd with us."You're not going to play Celtic and dominate the game for 90 minutes. We'll have spells, they'll have spells, it's just the way it is."I think it's important that we tap into having that 50,000 behind us and be behind the players, support them, have their backs, not be on their backs and really make it as tough for Celtic as possible."There's been a lot of frustration over a period of time at the club and it's up to us to try and show that we're going to deliver something a bit different."Celtic manager Martin O'Neill: "I suppose if you get in front in the game, that makes them anxious."Talking about getting in front and getting in front are two different things. The crowd will be right behind their team, which you would expect."We just do our best. We know that we're up against a very fine side. We're up against a crowd that can make a difference. "I'd be delighted to be celebrating something in the game."

schema.headline: Rangers v Celtic: What makes Sunday's League Cup quarter-final crucial?

title: Diljit Dosanjh: Punjabi singer makes history under the famous Wembley arch
description: On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously sta
body: On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived".But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase.Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said.Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said.And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from G.O.A.T. to Lover.Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran.He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet".His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star. Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him.In London, Dosanjh's crowd was largely - but not entirely - South Asian.The hype for his appearance was building all afternoon, with fans arriving early to get in place."MJ [Michael Jackson] and Madonna, he's that level for us," said one fan. "He's so good looking, and so down to earth," said another.When he came on the stage shortly after 8pm, dressed in traditional attire, the stadium erupted and the screams barely stopped for the next two-and-a-bit hours.Known for his high-energy performances, he wowed fans with his dance routines to songs including Hass Hass and Born to Shine.His soulful voice echoed around the stadium, demonstrating his range, as he blended homegrown Punjabi music with rap and hip-hop.Throughout the show, the audience waved lights, sang along and - of course - danced. At times, the standing area closest to the stage resembled an Indian wedding, with fans copying Dosanjh's impressive moves.But despite performing in such a vast venue, Dosanjh proved again his ability to connect on a personal level with fans.He brought a range of fans on stage, from young children to an elderly woman, taking selfies and giving them gifts.He also acknowledged those in the back rows of the 90,000-seater stadium, saying those at the back were "full of heart", and encouraged applause for them.There was also exciting news for fans in India, as he announced he would be performing in November at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad.The concert was capped off with the emotion of the night - his track Main Hoon Punjabi, which means "I am Punjab" - set to a spectacular firework display."What an incredible show, the energy  and vibe was unparalleled!" concert goers Amit and Rani told the BBC."We love Diljit and have been to all his shows in the UK. This was something else, a moment in time we won't forget being a part of."They added that it was not only a privilege "but a moment to celebrate for Punjabi culture".Dosanjh likes a "first".From humble beginnings as a small village boy from Punjab, he made history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi-language singer to perform at the US music festival Coachella.He also famously made his Met Gala debut decked in majestic Punjabi attire.His meteoric rise has seen him perform across America and Europe, and collaborate with pop stars from Sia to Sheeran.His authenticity is a big part of his appeal. He remains true to his Punjabi roots, wears his turban as a sign of pride, and sings in his mother tongue.Away from music, Dosanjh is also a popular Bollywood actor - and a social media sensation. Even those who haven't heard his music have probably viewed his funny Instagram videos - such as him arguing with an Amazon Alexa device, external that couldn't understand his accent.Now, he's performed on a stage that's previously been home to titans of music from Taylor Swift to Coldplay.For Dosanjh and his millions of global fans, it means Punjabi music, Punjabi culture and Punjabi vibrancy has reached an historic moment.Speaking to the BBC before his gig, he said he felt "thankful" to be here."When we were going to book this venue, everyone said, 'Think again before you book, it's a big stadium'," he said."I said: 'We'll see whatever comes. I want that our people are happy and can say yes, we can do this too!'"He reflected on the many artists who had performed there before him, adding that to follow their footsteps "means a lot, a lot"."It may not mean as much for someone like Harry Styles, as much as it means for us. He has performed on such stages, but for us, it's very special. Coming from a village to here - it's very special.""I feel good. I feel happy. And I feel good for my people. I feel good for the next generation," he said.And of course, there was only one way he could end."We are here. Punjabi Aa Gaye Oye!"

schema.headline: Diljit Dosanjh: Punjabi singer makes history under the famous Wembley arch

title: World Sepsis Day: Burnley boss Jackie Bachteler thought she would die during sepsis scare
description: Bachteler moved from San Diego to join Burnley's coaching staff in December 2025 and after a few weeks she thought jet lag and a busy schedule had led
body: Bachteler moved from San Diego to join Burnley's coaching staff in December 2025 and after a few weeks she thought jet lag and a busy schedule had led to a common cold.But she walked into the training ground one morning and "the whole room spun". She tried to get fresh air but was struggling to breathe.She instantly knew something was wrong and called for a club doctor. The men's team doctor was on site and checked her over.Her blood pressure dropped quickly and her oxygen levels were really low. She was immediately rushed to hospital and Bachteler feared the worst."To be honest, I thought I was going to die. I just had this feeling in my body like 'this is it'. I knew something was wrong," Bachteler told BBC Sport."They gave me some treatment for my lungs and then they tried to send me home, but I knew something wasn't right and asked them to do more."They checked my blood pressure and it just plummeted. Then I couldn't walk. I was so dizzy and really confused. I was getting blotches on my skin."They did a blood test and all of a sudden four or five doctors were sprinting towards me. I had two IVs with fluids and antibiotics, as well as [an] oxygen [mask]."Bachteler was given a room in the intensive care unit [ICU] for a couple of days as medical staff tested her blood every 20 minutes and her organs.Her family, from the United States, could not travel over, while her wife, based in Finland, was stuck in a snowstorm.Bachteler was alone in hospital and did not know fully what was going on."On my third day in hospital, I tried to stand up and I couldn't. The nurses told me not to walk and when you hear that it's a bit of an alarm bell," she said."It was just lung treatment after lung treatment, fluids after fluids, antibiotics and everything else. I had to get help to use the bathroom."It was close to when you face your mortality. It just gives you another perspective on life."Bachteler had to learn to walk again and put her coaching career on hold until Burnley welcomed her back in July as their new women's team manager.She is still not fully recovered and suffers with post-sepsis syndrome, which leads to dizzy spells and extreme fatigue.During a pre-season friendly a few weeks ago, Bachteler became unwell."It was so hot with the sun facing the bench. I got up in the second half and it was like when you have too much wine, you get up and you're like, 'woah!'"I was just so dizzy. I gave the instruction, talked to the team and then I went to the cafe on site and said to them: 'Can I sit in your freezer?'"I just needed to calm down. Then I started crying because my nervous system is still recovering and it's just been really, really hard."Bachteler praises Burnley's support throughout the process, saying that club doctors "saved her life" and have put her in touch with a respiratory specialist.She has received supportive messages from players and has been able to delegate jobs to her coaching staff, who she describes as "phenomenal".Her family have also supported her - but it has been mentally tough.Bachteler recalls a day in May when her parents flew over from the US and she had to leave a restaurant because of extreme dizziness."We went for Sunday dinner and it was loud. I just got so dizzy and they could see it. As we were walking back, I was shaking and I didn't know where I was," she said."They started crying, both of them. I think it was even harder for them. I get emotional any time I talk about my family with this."When my wife was able to see me [in hospital], she just started crying because of the amount of weight I lost."I'm really athletic and I'm really fit, but then I wasn't able to walk. She had to hold me up going down the stairs."Bachteler continues to have respiratory therapy to improve her lungs.She still struggles with fatigue, mental fog, memory loss and trembles if she becomes too exhausted, as well as suffering from regular dizzy spells."I'm definitely in a good way though. I'm about 70 to 80% Jackie again and that's thanks to the club, the doctors here and the NHS - but it was close."If I had gone home that day when the emergency room tried to send me back, I wouldn't be sitting here today."Bachteler says she leaves work every day thankful for a second chance and remains grateful to the support of staff members at Burnley.The near-death experience has helped put football into perspective too."A loss is a loss. I really believe in what I'm doing and in the people that I'm doing it with. Now the worst thing that will happen is that we lose a game," she said.Her experience will make Sunday's occasion at Turf Moor even more special and Bachteler hopes she can use it to raise awareness of the symptoms of sepsis."I realised it's a leading cause of death. I didn't even know what sepsis was before. I thought it was something you heard on Grey's Anatomy," said Bachteler."I didn't understand the severity of it and how much it's missed by doctors. The amount of people that have been affected really shocked me. It's a silent killer."Hopefully I can use the game as a tool to help others recognise the signs and let them know they are not alone. Over 50% of survivors have [post-sepsis syndrome]."To be standing on the pitch, doing something that I love, that I've dreamed of doing every single day and knowing that wouldn't have been the case almost a year ago, it's a bit poetic it's on World Sepsis Day."

schema.headline: World Sepsis Day: Burnley boss Jackie Bachteler thought she would die during sepsis scare

title: Five night sky events to look forward to this autumn
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, This year's November full moon will appear as a supermoon. This is 2025's November Beaver Moon captured above
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, This year's November full moon will appear as a supermoon. This is 2025's November Beaver Moon captured above forests in HungaryAutumn brings longer nights to the northern hemisphere, offering more opportunities to get outside and look up at the night sky.There is plenty to look out for over the coming months, from impressive meteor showers to dazzling star clusters.The series of spectacles begins with the Pleiades as the autumn nights draw in.It will be followed by the impressive Orionid meteor shower in late October, and a planetary parade, the Leonid meteor shower and a supermoon in November.The PleiadesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A view of the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters or Messier 45 (M45)As the nights lengthen through autumn, one of the most recognisable star clusters in the night sky becomes increasingly prominent.The Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters, is a cluster of young stars around 440 light years from Earth.Despite its name, most people can see around six stars with the naked eye, although many more become visible through binoculars or a telescope.Look towards the east during autumn evenings, where the Pleiades can be found in the constellation Taurus.Orionid meteor showerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Orionid meteor shower observed in the night sky on October 22, 2025 in Dezhou, Shandong Province of ChinaThe Orionid meteor shower is active from early October into November, reaching its peak around 21 October.Twice each year, Earth passes through trails of dust and debris left behind by Halley's comet. As these tiny particles enter Earth's atmosphere at high speed, they heat up and produce the streaks of light we see as meteors.The Orionids appear to radiate from the constellation Orion, which gives the shower its name.For the best chance of seeing them, find somewhere dark and away from artificial lights and allow your eyes time to adjust.November planetary paradeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jupiter and Venus are two of the planets which will be easy to see in the sky in mid-November. Early risers could be treated to a gathering of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter around 14 November.All four planets will be above the horizon before sunrise, although some will be easier to spot than others.Mercury will be particularly challenging because it remains low in the sky and close to the glare of the rising sun.Venus and Jupiter, meanwhile, are among the brightest objects in our night sky and should be much easier to pick out.Leonid meteor showerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, You don't need binoculars or a telescope to see meteors, just give your eyes sometime to adjust to looking up at the night sky.Another meteor shower arrives later in November, with the Leonids expected to peak around 17 November.The Leonids can travel at about 70km per second as they enter the Earth's atmosphere, making them some of the fastest meteors visible from Earth.Under ideal, dark sky conditions, around 10 to 15 Leonids an hour can be visible at the shower's peak, although the actual number seen will depend on weather, light pollution and the brightness of the Moon.They get their name from the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate. The best time to look is generally after midnight and before dawn, when Leo is higher in the sky.The Beaver supermoonImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A November supermoon rising over Bamburg Castle in Northumberland in 2016November's full moon is known as the Beaver Moon. The name is thought to come from the time of year when beavers were particularly active, preparing their lodges and storing food ahead of winter. It will also be a supermoon, reaching full phase on 24 November. A supermoon occurs when a full Moon is relatively close to Earth, making it appear slightly larger and brighter.The November supermoon is also the first of a run of four full Moons which can be classed as supermoons, running through to February 2027.Be sure to make the most of your autumn skywatching by checking the weather first on the BBC Weather app or online.

schema.headline: Five night sky events to look forward to this autumn

title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
description: Figure caption, 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AIByBrandon LivesayUpdated 1 hour agoAn artificial
body: Figure caption, 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AIByBrandon LivesayUpdated 1 hour agoAn artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.Jacob Coxon told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg on Saturday about his viral resignation post in which he raised concerns about out-of-control AI."I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.His resignation comes amid growing safety concerns in the industry, including from his former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, who in an essay argued for development to slow down.The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.Amodei said developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.The 27-year-old Coxon - who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic - welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale"."The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like.One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet.Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year.In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks."To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry."The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment"."This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said.Industry figures have suggested comments about the perils and power of AI may be designed to generate hype. Other critics say Anthropic has been trying to trigger a regulatory push to block competition, leaving it and OpenAI with a duopoly.Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a potentially record-setting initial public offering. OpenAI had been expected to do the same, but Altman said it would be an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine on Friday.Coxon's views have also been questioned by the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue."Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."After Amodei's essay was published on Saturday, however, Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by the Anthropic boss.Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs last week, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.Huang has previously said the notion that AI was "going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years. He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress". "They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology."But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives".His comments about AI have been shared millions of times on social media, with Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger responding on X that he agreed with Coxon."We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger said.Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.These warnings have become louder in recent weeks, as new models have exhibited more and more powerful capabilities that their creators may be struggling to control.Anthropic said in April that it was withholding its Mythos model from public use because it could independently escape the testing environment, known as a sandbox.OpenAI has also said certain aspects of its recent Astra model's development had been paused, citing cybersecurity concerns.

schema.headline: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC

title: PM's top security adviser says Europe faces hard winter to keep pressure on Putin
description: The UK national security adviser has said Europe must be ready to endure "real hardship" this winter if it is to keep up economic pressure on Russia.I
body: The UK national security adviser has said Europe must be ready to endure "real hardship" this winter if it is to keep up economic pressure on Russia.In rare public remarks, Jonathan Powell told a conference in Kyiv that Europe's strategy of supporting Ukraine and imposing sanctions on Moscow was working.Powell said talk of Russian escalation was "not a problem" but a "sign of success" that pressure on President Vladimir Putin was finally paying off - and as such European nations should not take their "foot off the gas".His optimistic remarks come as Russia continues to target Ukrainian infrastructure and as Europe faces a severe energy shortage this winter after drastically reducing its dependence on Russian oil and gas.Despite Russia's full-scale invasion now being in its fifth year, Powell said Ukraine had "already won" because Putin would not be able to seize the whole country and "a free Ukraine in Europe" would be able to choose its own direction regardless of any territorial loss.The prime minister's most senior security adviser was in Ukraine's capital only last weekend for talks with US President Donald Trump's envoys after they visited Putin in Moscow.His remarks at the Yalta European Strategy forum - to an audience of Ukraine's top leadership and international supporters - provided an unusual and detailed insight into UK policy on the war, and were distinctly positive compared to those of others.Round the clock Russian attacks on Ukraine are damaging the country's economy, weakening morale and raising fears about the coming winter when power shortages are expected.Oleksandr Kravchenko, Ukraine's minister of economy, told the conference that Russian attacks this year were expected to cost $10bn (£7.4bn) in destroyed infrastructure and assets. With the blockade of Ukraine's sea ports curbing grain exports, he said Ukraine's GDP would contract by 1.5%.Europe is now preparing for winter amid a global energy crisis and with low stockpiles of gas, making sanctioned Russian supplies of liquid natural gas potentially more attractive to some EU countries.Sanctions have meant Europe has massively reduced its consumption of Russian gas - but not entirely, with some countries dragging their feet. The EU still gets 12% of its gas imports from Russia but plans a complete phase-out by January. However, last week the European Court of Auditors said this plan was "faltering" amid gas shortages due to the Iran war.Powell said "we cannot turn that into an advantage for Putin", adding that pressure on Putin was working "and that means we have to keep the pressure up"."It will require some real hardship and difficulties on our parts," he added. "But we will have to swallow that and we have to keep the economic, military, political and diplomatic support going for Ukraine."While admitting that things in Ukraine did "feel a bit difficult at the moment", with a lack of Patriot air defence missiles, strikes on businesses and the governments budget deficit, Powell insisted "there are strong reasons for optimism".He said Trump – who has blown hot and cold on Ukraine – was "in a very different place". "He sees that Ukraine is doing better and therefore he is not leaning in the direction of Putin in the way that he was previously. I think that's a really big asset."Powell said Russia was no longer claiming the US had agreed that Ukraine should give up territory and hopes of Nato membership at last year's Trump-Putin summit in Alaska."The so-called Anchorage compromise is firmly dead," he said. "We can stop worrying about it. It's finished."This meant "we can look for serious ways of getting to a negotiated settlement, rather than waiting for the Ukrainian people to hand over territory the Russians have not been able to conquer", Powell said.Ukrainian commanders had successfully held the front line on the ground while Russia had reached 1.5 million casualties, Ukraine had increasingly struck deep within Russian territory while Europe's resolve remained solid, he noted."The strategy is to apply enough pressure to make [Putin] want to get into negotiation," Powell said."And I think that the escalation we hear talk about is not a problem - it's a sign of success, because what's happening is the pressure that we are putting on Putin is finally paying off."Putin himself has given little sign he is feeling under pressure, telling journalists earlier this month: "I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble."Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities have begun evacuating some residents in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, the biggest cities still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. Russia claims sovereignty over the Donbas and fully capturing it is a key objective for Moscow.Powell said the war was "not about territory" but about "the right of Ukraine to be independent", adding that "to the extent that [Putin] gains another 10km of land or loses another 40km of land, this war is already won"."That's the threat to him at home. There is a free, independent and European Ukraine, and people in Russia are going to notice that."The national security adviser said it was a "mug's game" to predict when the war might end, but said Europe had to be prepared to negotiate a settlement. "Where we least expect it, Putin will be ready to negotiate... It's all about getting him to be serious in that negotiation. And I think that strategy is beginning to work."Powell, who helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland, said the US and Europe should maintain contact with Putin – despite describing the Russian leader as a "terrorist"."What we don't want is miscalculation - that they don't understand where our red lines are. That's why I think it's important the CIA went to Moscow as well."

schema.headline: PM's top security adviser says Europe faces hard winter to keep pressure on Putin

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Nigel hits the jackpot' and 'Dark day for democracy'
description: Most of the papers feature details of the two huge donations to Reform UK on their front page, including the Sunday Times, external, which says the "u
body: Most of the papers feature details of the two huge donations to Reform UK on their front page, including the Sunday Times, external, which says the "unprecedented cash injection" has "stunned politics". Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, external, the second donor, Christopher Harborne, argues that Britain needs to regenerate after more than a decade of decline and says he believes Reform is "the only party" that can deliver economic prosperity. He insists he expects "nothing" in return for his donation which he describes as a "philanthropic gift" to the UK.Reform's leader, Nigel Farage, has told the Mail on Sunday, external that the donations of Harborne and Ben Delo "help to level a playing field that has always been tilted against any genuine challenge to the two-party duopoly". He stresses the money "will be used for one purpose only" - to ensure Reform is ready to form a government at the next election - adding that it will fund "the best research department British politics has ever seen", meaning policies are properly costed and workable.Several papers use their leader column to assess the donations. The Sunday Express, external says the funds have the potential to "transform" the next election race, calling them a "powerful show of support" for Nigel Farage and his party at a time when it faces controversies over funding. The Mail on Sunday suggests the donations "might just have changed the course of British politics for the better". It urges Farage to use the money to professionalise Reform and marginalise the chancers who invariably hang around new political movements.The Sunday Times urges caution, saying voters will have to wait for the Reform manifesto to find out whether mega-donors can buy influence. But the Observer already appears certain they can, warning that the gifts "are an insult to British democracy" and a "serious challenge to its integrity". The Sunday Mirror, external is also concerned. It says voters need to be reassured that national politics is not for sale to the highest bidder and that Britain's democracy "is not being hawked off to a couple of billionaires who seem to have more money than sense".Elsewhere, the Sun on Sunday, external reports that American spies have smuggled a paedophile who was working at the US embassy in London out of the UK without informing British police. It says the move has "sparked accusations of a cover-up" and prompted crisis meetings between Scotland Yard and senior ministers. The Metropolitan Police says it is liaising with US authorities about an investigation into suspected offences relating to indecent images of children.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Nigel hits the jackpot' and 'Dark day for democracy'

title: Insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
description: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hoste
body: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity. They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post."We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology."It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said."Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".  And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector.Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety."Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's  proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety. Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development."There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could.""When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic. OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".OpenAI, which announced in June that it would go public on the stock market, was most recently valued at $852bn.The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment.At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.One investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - CEO of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words."No," he said.

schema.headline: Insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley

title: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
description: "The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.Sh
body: "The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.She still fails to understand why Russian authorities could not stop Ukrainian soldiers storming two border checkpoints in August 2024, taking around 40 prisoners and bombing a convoy carrying Russian soldiers.Within six days they had overrun more than 777 sq km (300 sq miles) of Russian territory, as Ukraine's military sought to divert Russian forces away from their front-line offensive.For most of the next eight months, mobile and internet links were down.Russia's foreign ministry repeatedly accused Ukraine of war crimes against civilians: allegations rejected in Kyiv as completely unfounded.Nearly 200 Russians sent a letter to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the United Nations, asking them to organise a humanitarian corridor to evacuate civilians.It never happened and, by late autumn, battles raged as Russian forces sought to retake the territory.Lyubov and others who had lost contact with their loved ones began to form groups.One resident, whose family friends had also stayed behind, began compiling a list of people she saw on videos published by the Ukrainian military and journalists. Then she began detailing those believed to have died and where they were buried."At first, in a panic, you try to do something – anything – to find some sort of information," she said. "Taking action brings a certain sense of relief, and that's how you can cope with the stress."Soon about 1,000 names were on the list.Lyubov wrote to the Red Cross and Kursk interior ministry appealing for help, but had no response.Early in 2025, Russia's human rights commissioner published a list of 517 Kursk residents reported missing. The list mixed up names of the missing with those who were searching for them, and the families said it was like a "slap in the face"."Publishing something like this is the height of incompetence and a lack of basic respect for people," said one young woman whose parents had gone missing, in a video shared online.Heavy fighting had been reported in late 2024 in the village of Darino, where Lyubov and mother were from, and authorities said that 90% of it had been destroyed.The Russian military regained control of the village and then began evacuating those who had survived, and the bodies of those who had not.One of the evacuees got in touch with Lyubov, telling her she had lived with her mother for the past few weeks. Her mum had passed away, she explained, following a head injury in circumstances that remain unclear.A few other elderly people had also died, she said, unable to cope with wartime conditions.Lyubov waited in vain for her mother's body to be brought out, while other families had no idea if their relatives were alive or dead.People complained no-one was searching for their loved ones and that there was no single list of those missing.Lyubov heard that the bodies of neighbours who died alongside her mother had been taken away from Darino in April, but her mother's body was still missing.She tried and failed to get an answer from the authorities: "They wouldn't listen, and everyone just kept saying that it was dangerous there, and no-one was going to deal with it right now."The head of one local village council, Yuri Tkachev, was among volunteers who went to retrieve the bodies of civilians, from the streets or from nearby fields."It's hard for people to know – or rather not to know – what has happened to their loved ones, whether they're being held captive or have died, and where they died," he said.Body bags and fuel for vans taking part in the evacuations were paid for either by the volunteers themselves or with donations, but not by authorities.Although regional officials met the group searching for the missing several times in the second half of 2025, relatives complained it made little difference.Lyubov was still searching for her mother's body, until she visited the mortuary last October during a trip to the regional capital Kursk."I just asked: 'A woman born in 1949 from the village of Darino – are there any unidentified bodies?'"The official turned his laptop screen towards her and immediately she recognised her deceased mother in a photograph from April 2025.She was lying on her side in the street, her knees bent. Lyubov tried not to look too closely. She recognised her mum's face and an old jumper, which she wore while she worked.She had provided a DNA sample in January but was told it had been lost, so her mother's body had been in the mortuary unidentified for several months.She had wanted to bury her mother in their home village, but for now that is impossible, so she has been cremated and her ashes sit in Lyubov's apartment in Belgorod, about 100 miles away.She is bitter that the government failed to stop the incursion, that it did not evacuate residents when it could, and that it persuaded them the situation was not serious.Asked by the BBC to comment on this story, there was no response from the Kursk governor, Russia's human rights commissioner or the Russian Red Cross.The command of Ukraine's Territorial Defence Forces and Ukraine's human rights commissioner of Ukraine said all the civilians they had evacuated from Kursk region had been handed over to Russia.Lyubov thinks back to when she used to ride her bike across the border into Ukraine to shop for sausages, yarn and ice cream."We went to see them, and they came to see us. And now not one of these villages exists any more."

schema.headline: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion

title: 'Everywoman' statue unveiled on Trafalgar Square's Fourth Plinth
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Lady in Blue will sit atop the Fourth Plinth for two yearsA sculpture inspired by a desire to bring a con
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Lady in Blue will sit atop the Fourth Plinth for two yearsA sculpture inspired by a desire to bring a contemporary "everywoman" to Trafalgar Square has been unveiled on London's Fourth Plinth.Lady In Blue by New York artist Tschabalala Self, which pays homage to a young, metropolitan woman, is the 16th artwork to feature on the plinth since 1998.The  bronze and blue figure replaces Mil Veces un Instante (A Thousand Times in an Instant) by Teresa Margolles.The statue has been patinated with a pigment refined from Lapis Lazuli, a semi-precious stone that has been used by artists for millennia.Self said she had set out to put an ordinary contemporary Londoner on a site more usually associated with statues of monarchs and military commanders."My work Lady In Blue will bring to Trafalgar Square a woman that many can relate to," the artist said. "She is not an idol to venerate or a historic figurehead to commemorate."She is a woman walking forward into our collective future with ambition and purpose. She is a Londoner, who represents the city's spirit."Image source, EPA/ShuttershockImage caption, Tschabalala Self's design was picked to feature on the plinth for two yearsSelf was named as the winning artist in March 2024, alongside Andra Ursuta, whose work is due to go up on the plinth in 2028.Both were selected by the Fourth Plinth Commissioning Group, an independent panel chaired by the writer and curator Ekow Eshun.She said: "Lady In Blue transforms the everyday into the monumental."Tschabalala Self takes the familiar figure of a woman moving through the city and gives her an extraordinary presence at the heart of London."Justine Simons, the deputy mayor for culture and the creative industries, described the work as a striking addition to a historic part of the city.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The sculpture was unveiled on Thursday morningBorn in New York in 1990, Self works across painting, printmaking and sculpture, often using sewn and printed materials to build up depictions of the human figure.She held her first institutional exhibition in London and later showed her first major painting series in the city.The Fourth Plinth was left empty for more than 150 years after money ran out for an equestrian statue of William IV. The commissioning programme was started by the RSA in 1998 and the first work, Mark Wallinger's Ecce Homo, went up the following year. A new sculpture has been installed roughly every two years since.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
description: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each ot
body: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth. When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly. "All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked."They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'. "And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'. "At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook."'Remember me?' she asked. Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result."I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match". "I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister. "This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters. "It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be." Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago. It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters. "We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know." Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents."Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says."Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began."We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together. "There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says."I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

schema.headline: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters

title: Drag Race co-creator Fenton Bailey speaks out after BBC axe
description: Drag Race co-creator warns of TV representation 'crisis' after BBC drops showImage source, BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyImage caption, Drag Race UK jud
body: Drag Race co-creator warns of TV representation 'crisis' after BBC drops showImage source, BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyImage caption, Drag Race UK judges Michelle Visage, RuPaul Charles, Graham Norton and Alan CarrByJosh ParryLGBT & Identity ReporterThe co-creator of Drag Race has said there is a "crisis of representation" on TV, following the BBC's decision to axe the UK edition of the show.Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Fenton Bailey said he did not believe there was a "hidden agenda" behind the decision, but feared "vulnerable communities are going to be even more vulnerable".The move led viewers to raise concerns about the corporation's on-screen representation, after it also cancelled two LGBTQ+ dating shows.A spokesperson for the BBC said the decision was down to "significant financial pressures", as it attempts to make £500m of savings.Other shows being cancelled include Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank and Live at the Apollo, and more than 500 job losses have also been announced.World of Wonder (WOW) announced future series of Drag Race UK, including a new All Stars version, will be broadcast exclusively on the company's own streamer, WOW Presents Plus.BBC News spoke to Bailey, screenwriters, TV critics and former Drag Race contestants about the move and what it means for on-screen representation."Queer culture is vulnerable"When Drag Race UK launched in 2019, co-creator Fenton Bailey, who was born in Portsmouth but now lives in Los Angeles, said working with the national broadcaster felt like a "very special homecoming" for his production company, WOW.The US version of the show, co-created by RuPaul Charles, Bailey and his business partner Randy Barbato, had been on air for more than 10 years and was a runaway success, with dozens of Emmy awards and an international following. Fans were eagerly awaiting a UK series to showcase the unique British style of drag. Now, eight series and three spin-offs later, the programme will stop broadcasting on the BBC after the current series ends."Even at the best of times, queer culture is vulnerable and you can't take anything for granted," Bailey told BBC News. "Just because a door opened yesterday doesn't mean it won't be slammed shut the next."BBC News understands discussions to renew the BBC's deal with the show lasted months, with producers hopeful an agreement could be reached, but talks ultimately failed due to the scale of the savings the corporation is trying to make.Image source, Santiago Felipe/Getty ImagesImage caption, Randy Barbato (left), and Fenton Bailey (right) with Drag Race judge Ross MathewsBailey said it was a sign of the "horrible financial situations" broadcasters are currently facing."The team at the BBC are amazing and so passionate about the show, this is not an easy thing for any of the people I interacted with, or something they wanted to do," he added.Drag Race UK was consistently one of BBC Three's most popular offerings, but according to Barb Audiences data, while average viewing figures for the series rose between 2022 and 2024, overall they've fallen around 15% over the past four years, against a backdrop of declining TV viewing figures across the board.Bailey said the figures "haven't plummeted," but had instead fallen in line with other terrestrial TV shows, and said the number of viewers watching on social media had risen "because that's where the audience has gone."Following the announcement, some viewers speculated the show could be acquired by another UK broadcaster, but Bailey suggested the show's creators may prefer to go it alone."We love partnerships, but in this particular moment, having the freedom to make the show the way we want may be preferable to getting into bed with another broadcaster and potentially be in the same situation a few more seasons down the road."A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."'It feels like the drawbridge is pulling up'Image source, BBC / Guy LecyImage caption, The Vivienne rose to fame after becoming the first winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK in 2019Scott Bryan, TV critic and author of Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Television, says the move is indicative of just how severe the financial pressures facing broadcasters have become."I can imagine Drag Race is an expensive show to make," Bryan told the BBC, "I can see the pressures the BBC are under, but it's rather concerning in regards to queer storytelling."You see LGBTQ+ lives reflected on soaps and primetime dramas much more casually, but there still needs to be shows specifically catering to a queer audience, and it feels like very quickly the drawbridge is pulling up."Earlier this year the BBC announced LGBTQ+ dating shows I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl were also being cancelled. The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows, but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".Author and screenwriter Juno Dawson says viewers have begun to notice a "pattern".She said: "I think that's why perhaps eyebrows have been raised, because Drag Race hasn't been cancelled in isolation. A couple of other LGBTQ+ shows have gone as well."It's a shame this is happening at the BBC, because commercial channels don't necessarily have an obligation to represent all the communities in the UK, but the BBC does and it's supposed to represent all of us, including LGBTQ+ people."Image source, BBC/Hat Trick ProductionsImage caption, The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens would return for a third seriesThe BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens, which features predominantly LGBTQ+ characters, would be renewed for a third series, and it represents the community elsewhere through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Amandaland, Vigil and EastEnders.A recent report from GLAAD, an American advocacy organisation, found film representation had fallen for a third consecutive year, external and more than 200 LGBTQ+ TV characters would disappear from screens in 2026 because of cancellations, endings or limited-run series.While similar figures for the UK aren't collated, Dawson fears a shrinking television industry in the UK will make it harder for commissioners to make LGBTQ+ stories."So many of my personal shows have gotten right up to green light, but for lots of different reasons, different commissioners - not just at the BBC - have decided to back away."Nobody is ever going to say to you 'it's because it was too niche', but all I can keep doing is writing television that feels true to me and represents me and my life."'You come for the sparkles… but you're dealing with important topics'While Drag Race is known for its camp humour and glamour, most episodes also tackled serious topics, with contestants opening up about everything from non-binary and trans identities to substance abuse and the realities of living with HIV."There's something very clever about Drag Race," Dawson said, "because you come for the sequins and the sparkles, but actually under its surface, you're dealing with really big, heavy and important topics."Kate Butch, who competed on season five of Drag Race UK and on spin-off UK vs the World, told the BBC they fear a move away from a public service broadcaster could impact the show's ability to reach audiences with "important" messages.Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyImage caption, Former contestant Kate Butch said the show had changed their career "immeasurably""It's great the show is going to carry on and shine a spotlight on the amazing drag artistry the UK has to offer," they said, "but I do mourn the possibility of someone maybe just flicking through the channels and randomly finding it."Butch told BBC News that the show coming off the BBC may also bring some positive changes to the programme - including the possibility of prize money and sponsorships."It's a lot of effort to go on Drag Race, a lot of investment and emotional labour," they added, "so I hope the audience follows and keeps supporting the queens."Fenton Bailey says he's excited about the show's future on its own streaming platform."We may not have the resources that the BBC has, but the spirit of Drag and RuPaul's Drag Race is about making something out of nothing," he told the BBC. "As a community we can survive and thrive in less than optimal conditions."We have. We can. We will."
